plan.topic: ACOG's first guidance on GLP-1 medicines (semaglutide, tirzepatide) in pregnancy planning and breastfeeding (Oct 23, 2026)
plan.angle: Honest-uncertainty Short, credited 'ACOG Practice Advisory, Oct 23, 2026' and verified on acog.org. Open: 'On semaglutide or tirzepatide and thinking about pregnancy? It's a fair question, and the data is still limited.' ACOG advises clinicians to talk through the limited safety data and consider stopping these medicines 1–2 months before trying to conceive, as a plan made with your clinician. Why: they stay in the body a long time, and human pregnancy data is limited. Breastfeeding: if used, the baby's weight gain is closely monitored with the baby's clinician; ACOG advises against use when breastfeeding a preterm infant or newborn (use ACOG's exact wording). Calm context, labelled observational and credited to ACOG: early studies haven't shown a clear increase in major birth defects after accidental early exposure, which is not proof of safety. Tirzepatide can make birth control pills less reliable at times, so ask your prescriber about backup contraception. Unexpected pregnancy: tell your prescriber or OB-GYN right away, and they'll guide next steps. One GI line. 'Not personal advice' plus the full prescriber line, then 'follow for more'. 170 words or fewer, no emoji.
plan.working_title: Semaglutide or Tirzepatide and Pregnancy: What OB-GYNs Advise #shorts
plan.why:
Fresh guidance from a major medical society (Oct 23) answers a high-intent question for a big part of our audience, and it tests the honest-uncertainty format behind our best Reel. It adds a new fact beyond the 10-15 carousel. | fact-check: Checked through Healio (23 Oct 2026). It's an ACOG Practice Advisory, written for clinicians. ACOG's wording: counsel patients about the lack of safety data and 'consider discontinuing GLP-1s 1–2 months before conception'. In lactation: shared decision-making, and 'closely monitor neonatal weight gain, in conjunction with the infant's clinician, if GLP-1s are used during breastfeeding'. It also advises against use in people breastfeeding preterm infants or neonates. On birth defects: 'early observational studies have not demonstrated a clear increase in major congenital malformations following inadvertent first-trimester exposure'. That is ACOG's line, so credit it to ACOG, not to 'consensus guidance'. The scriptwriter must confirm all of this on acog.org itself before scripting. It's a high-value safety topic for the audience.
Two fixes:
(1) Keep ACOG's verb 'consider stopping, with your clinician'. Never say 'ACOG says stop'.
(2) Remove 'don't stop or change your medicine on your own' from the unexpected-pregnancy line. The semaglutide and tirzepatide labels tell clinicians to discontinue when pregnancy is recognised, so that line could delay action. Use 'tell your prescriber or OB-GYN right away; they'll guide next steps, including diabetes care if you have it'.
Also add the tirzepatide label point that it can make birth control pills less reliable at times, and say 'ask your prescriber about backup contraception'. Don't give a schedule. Keep it calm, with no emoji and no 'Ozempic babies'.

package.title: Semaglutide, Tirzepatide & Pregnancy: ACOG's New Advice #shorts
package.description:
ACOG's October 23, 2026 advisory: clinicians should consider stopping semaglutide or tirzepatide one to two months before conception, planned together with you; human pregnancy data is limited. ACOG advises against use while breastfeeding preterm or newborn babies. Nausea is common with both; tirzepatide can make birth control pills less reliable for four weeks after starting or a dose increase, so ask your prescriber about a non-oral or backup method.

Not personal advice. Don't stop or change your medicines on your own. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

Thinking about pregnancy while on semaglutide or tirzepatide? You're not the only one asking.

On October 23, 2026, ACOG — the U.S. obstetricians' group — issued a practice advisory on GLP-1 medicines in pregnancy and breastfeeding.

Here's what it says:
→ Clinicians should consider stopping these medicines 1–2 months before conception, planned together with you (the Wegovy label says at least 2 months for semaglutide)

factcheck.summary: The core facts check out against Healio's 23 Oct 2026 report on the ACOG practice advisory. That includes: considering stopping 1–2 months before conception; advising against use when breastfeeding preterm infants or newborns; if a GLP-1 is used while breastfeeding, closely monitoring the baby's weight gain with the infant's clinician; and early observational studies showing no clear increase in major birth defects after accidental first-trimester exposure, with data still limited. The Zepbound label (section 7.2) and Lilly Medical both confirm the 4-week oral-contraceptive window after starting and after each dose increase, with a switch to a non-oral method or an added barrier method. The Zepbound label also confirms nausea as the most common side effect (about 25–29% versus 8% on placebo). The Wegovy PDF is reachable but didn't parse as text. Its 'at least 2 months before a planned pregnancy' line is standard label wording, kept here on that basis. I couldn't find the ACOG primary document online, so Healio stays the source for ACOG. Fixes needed: s8 credits 'not for use during pregnancy' to ACOG, which the source doesn't support; the on-screen 'why' line applies semaglutide's washout reasoning to both drugs; s2 names tirzepatide as covered without a source; the Short runs about 205 words against the 170-word rule. Safety framing is good: no dosing, a clinician at every step, the disclaimer and prescriber line are both present, and the hook pays off.

issues.claim: Labels and ACOG: not for use during pregnancy; your clinician guides next steps
issues.problem: The Healio report has ACOG saying to counsel patients about the lack of safety data and to consider stopping 1–2 months before conception. It doesn't quote ACOG saying 'not for use during pregnancy'. The labels say to discontinue when pregnancy is recognized. So the line credits ACOG with something it didn't say, and it's stronger than the narration (fails the muted-viewer test).
issues.fix: Replace the item with: "Labels: stop when pregnancy is recognized; your prescriber guides next steps (Wegovy and Zepbound Prescribing Information)". Remove ACOG from this item's attribution.

issues.claim: Why: they stay in the body a long time
issues.problem: The Wegovy label gives semaglutide's long washout period as the reason for its 2-month gap. Neither the Zepbound label nor the Healio report gives that reason for tirzepatide, so 'they' stretches a semaglutide-only reason to both drugs.
issues.fix: Replace with: "Why (Wegovy label): semaglutide has a long washout period".

issues.claim: GLP-1 medicines, including semaglutide and tirzepatide
issues.problem: The Healio report describes the advisory as covering GLP-1 medicines in general and names only semaglutide as an example. Nothing in the source confirms that tirzepatide is named.
Over the 170-word Shorts limit, which counts the prescriber line.
issues.fix: s2 narration: "On October twenty-third, twenty twenty-six, the U-S obstetricians' group A-C-O-G issued new advice on G-L-P-one medicines in pregnancy and breastfeeding." s3: cut "planned together with you" and end with "Pregnancy data is limited." s6: "The catch: tirzepatide can make birth control pills less reliable for four weeks after starting and after each dose increase. Ask your prescriber about a backup method." s8: "Pregnant unexpectedly? Tell your prescriber or O-B-G-Y-N right away." Keep s9 unchanged.

issues.claim: tirzepatide can make birth control pills less reliable for four weeks after starting and after each dose increase
issues.problem: Accurate, but the label wording is about hormonal pills specifically (from slower stomach emptying). Viewers on semaglutide injection might assume the same rule applies to them, and the on-screen text doesn't say where the rule comes from.
issues.fix: On-screen text: "Tirzepatide label: birth control pills may be less reliable for 4 weeks after starting and after each dose increase". Add the attribution: "Zepbound Prescribing Information, section 7.2; Lilly Medical".

Trimmed a handful of redundant/duplicate swooshes and blips in dense clusters (t≈22, 26.5, 31, 58, 67) and pulled down a few cues that were sitting slightly hotter than the speech-SFX window (-13 to -13.6 dB) at t≈19.7, 31, 67.5 and 88.2. Added five bespoke, restrained musical stingers at the hook, the ACOG advisory, the early-research mention, the 'encouraging, not proof' turn, and the closing safety line to give the story's key beats a felt lift without ever competing with the voice.
